interviewQuestions.question: How do you fix a deadlock from two threads locking two mutexes in opposite order?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd fix it by attacking the circular-wait condition directly: establish one fixed, global order for the two locks — say, always acquire `mutexA` before `mutexB`, everywhere in the codebase — and change whichever code path acquires them in the wrong order to match. With both threads now required to request `mutexA` first, whichever one gets it simply blocks the other from proceeding at all; there's no longer a scenario where each thread holds one lock while wanting the other, since both threads always request in the same order.

I'd explain why this is the right attack point rather than the other three Coffman conditions: I can't remove mutual exclusion (the locks protect real shared state), attacking hold-and-wait would mean redesigning to acquire both locks atomically upfront (extra complexity, and it can hurt utilization if the second lock isn't needed until much later), and attacking no-preemption would need rollback support neither critical section has. Lock ordering, by contrast, needs zero new synchronization primitives — it's a pure discipline change.

For a real codebase, I'd also flag that this needs to be enforced everywhere the two locks are used together, not just in the one bug I found — a single other code path acquiring them in reverse order reintroduces the exact same bug. I'd mention tools like Linux's `lockdep` that catch ordering violations automatically.

**Testing:** whether you go straight to the practical, broadly-applicable fix (lock ordering) rather than a theoretically-correct-but-impractical one, and whether you think about codebase-wide enforcement, not just the one bug report.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fixing a two-mutex deadlock

interviewQuestions.question: Why do most real systems attack circular wait via lock ordering rather than attacking one of the other three Coffman conditions?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the other three attack points each carry a cost that doesn't generalize well, while lock ordering's cost — needing consistent acquisition-order discipline — is manageable in most real codebases. Attacking mutual exclusion only works when the resource can genuinely be made shareable, which fails for anything correctness-sensitive like a mutable counter or a printer. Attacking hold-and-wait, via acquiring every needed resource upfront, requires knowing your full resource needs in advance — often impossible for interactive or data-dependent workloads — and can tank utilization by forcing a process to hold resources long before it actually uses them. Attacking no-preemption requires the resource's state to be cleanly savable and restorable, which works for CPU registers or memory pages but not for a half-completed external side effect or a physical operation like printing.

Lock ordering, by contrast, needs no advance knowledge of future resource needs and doesn't require resources to be preemptible — it's a static rule about the order in which acquisition happens, enforceable at code-review or tooling level (a runtime lock-order checker like Linux's `lockdep`) rather than requiring a redesign of how resources are requested or released.

I'd add the honest caveat: it's not free — it requires the discipline to hold across the entire codebase, including rare error paths and third-party code, and a single violation anywhere reintroduces the exact vulnerability it was meant to close.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the real trade-offs across all four attack points, not just default to naming lock ordering without understanding why the alternatives are worse in practice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why lock ordering wins in practice

interviewQuestions.question: Your team enforces lock ordering by convention (documented in comments), but a production incident revealed a rarely-hit code path violating it. How would you prevent this class of bug going forward?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat this as a signal that documentation alone isn't sufficient enforcement for an all-or-nothing invariant — a comment doesn't stop a developer six months later from adding a new code path that acquires the same two locks in reverse order, especially in an error-handling branch that's rarely exercised in testing.

Concretely, I'd add runtime lock-order tracking if the language/runtime supports it — the Linux kernel's `lockdep` is the canonical example: it tracks the actual order locks get acquired in across all executed code paths and immediately flags an inconsistency the first time it's exercised, even if that particular run didn't actually deadlock. Some userspace threading libraries and static analyzers offer similar checks (Rust's borrow checker catches some classes of this at compile time for certain patterns; Go's race detector and various C/C++ tools like TSan can catch related issues at runtime).

I'd also push for the ordering rule to be encoded structurally where possible rather than left as a convention — for instance, wrapping the multi-lock acquisition in a single helper function that always acquires in the correct order internally, so callers can't get the order wrong even if they wanted to, rather than relying on every call site remembering the rule.

Finally, I'd add the specific reversed-order code path from the incident as a regression test, and treat any future `lockdep`-style warning as a build-blocking failure, not just a log line to notice later.

**Testing:** whether you reach for enforcement mechanisms (tooling, structural encoding) instead of just 'we'll document it better' after an incident like this.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Enforcing lock ordering after an incident
